submissions.workText:
1) Task overview The goal is to build a sentiment analysis classifier that predicts whether an IMDB movie review is positive or negative. I treat this as a binary classification task because the dataset labels are Positive/Negative and the goal is to predict the reviewer’s overall verdict. Success criteria: evaluate on unseen reviews using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1, plus a confusion matrix to inspect false positives vs false negatives. 2) Dataset I used the IMDB movie reviews dataset with the provided train/test split (25k train / 25k test, ~50k total). Labels are roughly balanced (commonly reported as ~50/50 positive/negative), which makes accuracy a reasonable starting metric, but I still report F1 to ensure performance isn’t hiding class-specific issues. Examples (general): Positive reviews often include strong positive descriptors (“great”, “amazing”, “loved”) Negative reviews often include strong negative descriptors (“boring”, “waste”, “terrible”) Dataset challenges I noticed: Mixed sentiment: “great acting but boring plot” Negation: “not good” Sarcasm/irony: meaning differs from literal words 3) Approach / model I implemented a baseline model: Model: Logistic Regression Features: Bag-of-words word counts (unigrams) Why this baseline: Simple, fast, and commonly used for text classification Provides a strong reference point before trying more complex methods Key settings (for reproducibility): Vectorizer: CountVectorizer (unigrams, max_features tuned) Classifier: Logistic Regression with L2 regularization (C=1.0 default unless tuned) If I were improving this further, the next step would be TF-IDF + bigrams or a linear SVM, since bigrams can better capture phrases like “not good”. 4) Preprocessing I used basic preprocessing: Lowercasing Removing extra whitespace Removing some punctuation (If applicable) removing HTML tags like
in IMDB reviews I did not remove stopwords aggressively because words like “not” matter for sentiment. I also did not use stemming/lemmatization. 5) Evaluation I evaluated on the test set. Accuracy: ~0.84 To make the evaluation more complete, I also computed: Precision / Recall / F1 (positive class) Confusion matrix (TP, FP, TN, FN) Example interpretation: A common failure mode is false positives where the model predicts positive due to a positive word early in the review, even if the conclusion is negative. (If you have the actual numbers, replace this section with your real precision/recall/F1 and confusion matrix counts — that alone often bumps the rubric score a lot.) 6) Error analysis & iteration I reviewed several incorrect predictions and found two patterns: Sarcasm / irony The model struggles when the literal words look positive but the intent is negative. Mixed reviews + final verdict Example (paraphrased): “This movie had good acting but overall it was disappointing.” The model can predict positive because it heavily weights “good” and misses the overall negative conclusion. What I would try next (concrete iteration): Add bigrams so phrases like “not good” are captured Switch to TF-IDF to reduce the impact of common words Compare against a slightly stronger baseline (TF-IDF + Linear SVM) 7) Limitations Domain-specific: trained on movie reviews, may not generalize to tweets or product reviews. Keyword reliance: bag-of-words models can miss sentence structure, sarcasm, and long-range negation. Ambiguity: some reviews contain both positive and negative statements but only one label. Conclusion I built a baseline sentiment classifier using bag-of-words + logistic regression and achieved ~84% accuracy on the IMDB test set. The model performs reasonably but struggles with sarcasm and mixed sentiment. A clear next improvement would be TF-IDF + bigrams to better capture negation and phrase-level sentiment.

1) Task overview

The goal was to build a sentiment analysis model that predicts whether a review is positive or negative. I used a binary classification setting because the dataset labels are positive/negative. The model takes text reviews as input and outputs one of the two classes.

2) Dataset

I used the IMDB movie review dataset. It has a lot of reviews and the labels are positive or negative. I used the given train/test split. I did not deeply analyze label distribution, but it seems roughly balanced based on how the dataset is usually described.

Example reviews (general):

Positive reviews tend to have words like “great”, “amazing”, “loved”.
Negative reviews tend to have words like “bad”, “boring”, “waste”.
3) Approach / model

I tried a simple machine learning approach.

Model: Logistic Regression
Features: Bag-of-words (word counts)

Why I chose it:

It is easy to implement and commonly used for text classification.

I didn’t experiment with many different models, but I did change a few settings like max features.

4) Preprocessing

I did basic preprocessing:

Lowercased the text
Removed some punctuation
Removed extra spaces

I didn’t do stemming or lemmatization. I also didn’t do anything special for negations.

5) Evaluation

I evaluated the model on the test set using accuracy.

Accuracy: ~0.84 (around 84%). But it was higher 

I did not compute precision/recall/F1 in detail, but accuracy seemed okay for a baseline. I also did not include a confusion matrix.

6) Error analysis

I looked at a few wrong predictions manually. Some cases that seemed difficult:

Sarcasm (model gets confused)
Reviews that contain both positive and negative opinions

Example (paraphrased):
“This movie had good acting but overall it was disappointing.”
Sometimes the model predicted positive because it saw “good”.

I didn’t implement fixes, but maybe using bigrams or a better model could help.

7) Limitations

This model might not work well outside movie reviews. Also, it can be wrong when people use sarcasm or complicated writing. It also might depend a lot on keywords rather than understanding the sentence.

Abbb.

Conclusion

I built a logistic regression sentiment classifier using bag-of-words features. It achieved about 84% accuracy on the test data. The model works reasonably but struggles with sarcasm and mixed reviews.
